The highest savings rate may apply to only one slice: calculate the interest before comparing accounts

Use four charts to translate a hypothetical tiered deposit schedule into annual interest dollars, a blended rate and a same-balance comparison with a flat rate.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Calculate interest by balance slice before comparing the average rate

Interactive planning lab

Annual interest from the three balance slices$450

Annual interest: tiered schedule less the entered flat-rate comparison-$75

Original hypothetical one-year deposit illustration, not a bank quote. A constant balance is held for a full year. Simple annual interest is paid once at the end, with no intra-year compounding, deposits, withdrawals, fees, tax, promotional window or balance qualification test. The first CAD 5,000 earns 1%; the next CAD 5,000 earns 3%; only the amount above CAD 10,000 earns the entered top rate. Crossing a threshold never reprices earlier slices. The comparison applies its entered flat rate to the same entire balance for the same full year. The blended rate is total annual interest divided by that balance. Actual accounts may use different tiers, all-balance rules, daily calculations, monthly credits or eligibility conditions. All rates and thresholds here are constructed assumptions, and no actual deposit-insurance eligibility, access terms or product recommendation is provided.

The central idea

The rate table needs an allocation rule. A high rate on the final balance slice does not reprice the dollars that remain in earlier slices.

01

Ask which dollars receive each rate

A savings-rate table can list several percentages without showing how much interest a particular balance will earn. The missing detail is the allocation rule: does a higher rate apply to the entire balance after a threshold is met, or only to dollars within a specified slice?

The FCAC savings-account guide distinguishes those possibilities and recommends checking the agreement. Its discussion also explains that actual accounts can differ in calculation and payment timing.

The interactive example uses progressive balance slices for a constant deposit held for one full year. It does not model an all-balance repricing rule or reproduce any bank’s offer.

02

Allocate the deposit before multiplying by a rate

The invented schedule pays 1% on the first CAD 5,000, 3% on the next CAD 5,000 and the entered top rate on any balance above CAD 10,000. The default deposit is CAD 15,000 and the top rate is 5%.

The first CAD 5,000 generates CAD 50 of annual interest. The next CAD 5,000 generates CAD 150. The final CAD 5,000 generates CAD 250. Adding those amounts gives CAD 450, before the excluded taxes and fees.

Every dollar of principal is assigned once. Crossing CAD 10,000 changes the rate applying to the next dollar; it does not change the rate already assigned to the first CAD 10,000.

03

Divide total interest by the whole balance to find the blended rate

The default blended rate is CAD 450 ÷ CAD 15,000 = 3%. It is below the 5% rate paid on the highest slice because two-thirds of the deposit earns lower rates.

This is a balance-weighted rate. Averaging 1%, 3% and 5% happens to produce 3% in the default example because the three slices contain equal amounts. With a different deposit, a simple average of the listed rates will generally give the wrong result.

For example, CAD 10,000 earns CAD 200, a 2% blended rate. CAD 25,000 earns CAD 950 at the default top rate, a 3.8% blended rate. The schedule has not changed; the weight of each occupied slice has.

04

Reconcile the tempting all-at-top-rate calculation

Applying 5% to the entire default CAD 15,000 produces CAD 750. The tiered rule pays CAD 450. The waterfall explains the CAD 300 difference without treating it as a fee.

The first CAD 5,000 earns four percentage points less than the top rate: CAD 200 less interest. The next CAD 5,000 earns two percentage points less: CAD 100 less. Subtracting both adjustments from CAD 750 produces the correct CAD 450.

A balance below CAD 10,000 has no money in the top slice at all. The label on the highest tier does not, on its own, describe the average rate earned by that smaller deposit.

05

Compare annual interest at the same balance and holding period

The default alternative applies 3.5% to all CAD 15,000 for the same full year. It generates CAD 525. The tiered schedule generates CAD 75 less in this particular comparison, even though its top rate is higher.

The matrix repeats the comparison across balances and flat rates. Within each cell, both rules use exactly the same principal and year. Differences in access, account fees, taxes, promotional duration or qualification terms are excluded rather than assumed equal in a real account decision.

The curve shows why the balance matters. Each additional dollar above CAD 10,000 earns 5% at the default input, but the blended rate approaches that top rate gradually because the earlier slices remain in the account. There is no sudden repricing of the existing deposit.

06

Use the actual agreement and cash calendar for the final budget

The model holds the balance constant and pays simple interest once at year-end. Actual accounts may calculate interest on daily balances, credit it monthly, compound it or require other conditions. A quoted rate needs those details before it becomes an annual cash estimate.

For a household plan, first identify the amount that can remain deposited and when it may be needed. Then calculate interest using the applicable balance rule and payment calendar. Account access and a bill’s due date still matter even when two options have similar annual interest totals.

Use the calculated dollars and any applicable costs or taxes to update the budget. The highest percentage in a rate table is a starting point for reading the terms, not a complete forecast of spendable interest.
